title: ⚔️ Peoples & Cultures
rawNotionMarkup: This page records the established intelligent peoples, broad cultural groupings, demographic notes and the common personality reputations associated with them. These descriptions are a starting point for worldbuilding and NPC characterisation, not biological laws. ## Shared principles - Eryndor contains many intelligent peoples with distinct histories, societies, customs and political interests. - No people is inherently good or evil, intelligent or foolish, civilised or savage. - Cultural reputation, species traits, individual personality and political allegiance are different things. Do not conflate them. - Individuals vary by region, family, class, profession, religion, education, upbringing, personal history and circumstance. - Some peoples are organised into kingdoms or large civilisations; others may have local, mobile, seasonal, clan-based, forest, coastal or other social structures. Do not assume every people has a conventional monarchy or state. - The sentient animal peoples are fully intelligent peoples with their own societies, not ordinary animals wearing clothes. They coexist alongside ordinary animals and livestock. An animal-like appearance alone does not establish whether a particular creature is an ordinary animal or a sentient person; establish this in context rather than assuming. - The personality descriptions below are cultural reputations and tendencies. Other peoples may misunderstand or exaggerate them. They can inform humour, prejudice, diplomacy, conflict or subversion, but they are not objective rules for every individual. ## Major ancient civilisations ### Khazari — dwarves - Population: Approximately 24 million. - Common lifespan: Approximately 300–450 years. - Political organisation: Seven powerful, culturally distinct and politically independent Mountain Thrones. - Established character: Proud, stubborn, practical, industrious and loyal. Craftsmanship, family, tradition, hard work and keeping one's word are highly respected. - Cultural tendencies: Long memories, serious grudges, dry humour, strong food and drink traditions, engineering, mining, metalwork, stonework and things built to last. - Important distinction: The Seven Thrones are not one uniform kingdom. Local law, customs, politics, dialect and identity can differ significantly. - Current campaign centre: Karak-Varn, one of the Seven Thrones. ### Eldar — elves - Population: Approximately 18 million. - Common lifespan: Approximately 700–1,200 years. - Political organisation: Several royal houses gathered under a High Sovereign in the western forests of Letharion. - Established character: Graceful, perceptive, intelligent, patient and artistic. Beauty, knowledge, history, etiquette and precision are valued. - Cultural reputation: Famously formal and exacting in manners and language. They may be exquisitely courteous while making disagreement feel like a surgical dissection. Their long memories can preserve both promises and old insults. - Variation: Some Eldar are traditionalists; others reject etiquette, speak bluntly, or use manners as political theatre. Do not make all Eldar smug, infallible or interchangeable. ### Urakai — orcs - Population: Approximately 31 million. - Political organisation: Sophisticated clan confederations across eastern plains and highlands; they are a rising civilisation. - Established character: Fierce, direct, proud, competitive and passionate. Courage, strength, endurance, loyalty and achievement are admired. - Cultural tendencies: Plain speaking, respect for those who stand their ground, strong family, clan and comrade loyalties. - Political context: Their ancient rivalry with the Khazari is political, territorial, industrial and military. Trade and alliances remain possible. - Important distinction: Urakai societies are sophisticated, not primitive, and the people are not inherently villainous. ## Other established peoples ### Drakari — true dragons - Population: Fewer than 10,000. - Organisation: Ancient courts and territories. - Common character reputation: Ancient, intelligent, proud, territorial and self-possessed. Knowledge, power, reputation, independence and ancient obligations matter to them. - Variation: Some are noble, philosophical and patient; others are vain, possessive, cruel or obsessively proud. They are individuals with histories and interests, not interchangeable monsters. ### Aelwyn — Fae - Organisation: Ancient seasonal courts and pacts. - Common character reputation: Enigmatic, whimsical, beautiful, unpredictable and deeply bound to old customs. - Cultural tendencies: Riddles, bargains, symbolism, ceremony and unusual hospitality. Promises, names, gifts and obligations may carry implications that outsiders do not understand. - Variation: Do not assume all Aelwyn are malicious or deceptive. Some may be generous, curious, solemn or sincerely devoted to their customs. ### Halflings Friendly, sociable, humble, cheerful, hospitable and fond of comfort. They value meals, family, gardens, stories, familiar places and local gossip. They may prefer peace and ordinary pleasures to danger, but can be brave, resourceful and stubborn when home or loved ones are threatened. Comfort-seeking is not cowardice. ### Gnomes Curious, inventive, clever, eccentric and inquisitive. They are drawn to mechanisms, puzzles, experiments, obscure knowledge and overlooked problems. Their ingenuity can be extraordinary, though enthusiasm can outrun caution. Some are meticulous theoreticians; others are chaotic tinkerers. ### Goblins Opportunistic, crafty, suspicious, quick-witted and resourceful. They value survival, cleverness, useful possessions, information and knowing when to retreat. They may be irreverent and fond of bargains. Goblin communities can be fiercely protective of their own; not every goblin is dishonest. ### Ents Patient, contemplative, ancient, deliberate and deeply connected to the natural world. They tend to think in seasons, generations and centuries. They protect forests and living things, may be slow to anger, and can be immense when roused. Individual temperaments still differ. ### Centaurs Independent, proud, athletic, adventurous and freedom-loving. They value open spaces, skill, kinship, personal honour and freedom of movement. They may be blunt and competitive, and impatient with cramped cities or excessive restrictions. They can be scouts, hunters, messengers, warriors, scholars, diplomats or artisans. ### Merfolk Proud, perceptive, adaptable and deeply aware of tides, currents and the changing sea. Navigation, memory, tradition, community and knowledge of the waters can be important. Some regard surface-dwellers as noisy, clumsy or ignorant of the ocean; others may be welcoming traders, curious travellers or skilled intermediaries. Their communities vary. ### Giants Powerful, independent, blunt, proud and sometimes slow to trust. They may value strength, endurance, hospitality and respect for territory. Their scale and possible longevity can shape their outlook, but do not make them simple-minded. Some are solitary and contemplative; others live in close-knit mountain or highland communities. Their size is not a personality. ## Rare colossal sentient beings ### Living Mountains Living Mountains are genuine, exceedingly rare colossal living beings. While dormant, their bodies can be indistinguishable from ordinary mountain ranges or solitary peaks. They may sleep for centuries or millennia, with forests, rivers, caves, snow and even settlements accumulating across them. Their movements and timescales are almost impossible for smaller peoples to comprehend. It is not established that they share one temperament or a common psychology. An individual might be contemplative, indifferent, protective, curious, wary or incomprehensible to smaller beings; these are possibilities for individual characterisation, not fixed species traits. They are not automatically benevolent, hostile, wise or interested in mortals. Most people will never witness one awaken, and reliable evidence is scarce. Their number, locations, origins, names and individual personalities remain unknown. Classification boundary: Living Mountains are included because they are sentient colossal life, but they are not a conventional widespread species or ordinary monster type. They are distinct from Giants and Ents. Do not make them convenient mounts or weapons, or connect one to Gloin or the eastern mine without a properly developed reason. ## Humans and the five major cultural groupings Humans are adaptable, ambitious, inventive, emotional and politically complicated. Their shorter lifespans often encourage urgency, energetic change and a desire to leave a legacy. The five major power groupings below have broad cultural reputations; none describes every human in that region. ### Aldermere Stubborn, practical, duty-bound and community-minded. They tend to admire courage, loyalty, hard work and keeping one's word. They often respect proof through action more than grand promises. ### Valtoria Disciplined, ambitious, hierarchical and politically calculating. They value order, military achievement, status, efficiency and national strength. Court and military life can be intensely competitive; personal loyalties and rivalries still matter. ### Northern Holds Hardy, blunt, resilient and cautious with outsiders until trust is earned. They value survival, kinship, hospitality, endurance and practical competence. They are not all grim or humourless. ### Merchant Republics Cunning, persuasive, cosmopolitan and commercially minded. They value opportunity, negotiation, information, wealth and recognising a good bargain. Commercial calculation does not exclude honour, generosity or sincere friendship. ### Southern Sultanates Cultured, scholarly, proud, hospitable and politically sophisticated. They value poetry, learning, trade, architecture, ceremony, reputation and refined debate. Hospitality may be elaborate; courtly life can involve subtle competition and diplomacy. These societies are not monolithic. ## Sentient animal peoples These peoples have their own families, societies, traditions and political interests. Animal traits may influence senses, instincts, movement or physical behaviour, but they are not simply animals wearing clothes. ### Wolvenkin Loyal, disciplined, protective, perceptive and community-oriented. They value trust, family, teamwork and earned respect. They may be alert to changes in their surroundings and slow to forgive betrayal. Pack-like bonds may inform social life, but not every community is organised identically. ### Foxfolk Clever, charming, curious, adaptable and mischievous. They enjoy wit, negotiation, exploration and unexpected solutions. Their reputation for trickery is sometimes deserved, but cleverness can also serve scholarship, diplomacy, invention and survival. ### Lionfolk Proud, courageous, commanding and protective, with concern for honour and dignity. They may value leadership, reputation, bravery and responsibility for those under their protection. Pride can inspire courage or become stubbornness and sensitivity to disrespect. ### Tigerfolk Independent, patient, confident, intense and calculating. They may favour precision over bluster and prefer to act on their own terms. Their confidence can be quiet; they may observe for a long time before committing. They are not all solitary or cold. ### Elephantfolk Thoughtful, patient, community-minded, strong-willed and long-remembering. They may value family history, accumulated wisdom, diplomacy and responsibility to the wider community. They can be difficult to rush or persuade to abandon a deeply held belief. ### Bearfolk Steady, strong, dependable, protective and often easy-going. They may value comfort, family, personal space and practical solutions. They dislike needless trouble but can be formidable when pushed too far. They are not all slow, sleepy or simple. ### Cowfolk Patient, sociable, hardworking, generous and community-oriented. They may value agriculture, craftsmanship, hospitality, stability and mutual support. Their gentle reputation can cause outsiders to underestimate their resilience, determination or strength. ### Pigfolk Sociable, resourceful, practical, pleasure-loving and shrewd. They may appreciate food, trade, family, celebrations, comfort and a good bargain. They can be blunt, stubborn and protective of their interests. Do not reduce them to gluttony or greed. ## Population and lifespan register Only record figures that are established; do not infer missing demographics. | People | Approximate population | Common lifespan | | --- | --- | --- | | Khazari | 24 million | 300–450 years | | Eldar | 18 million | 700–1,200 years | | Urakai | 31 million | Not established here | | Drakari | Fewer than 10,000 | Not established here | | Aelwyn | Not established | Not established | | Halflings | Not established | Not established | | Gnomes | Not established | Not established | | Goblins | Not established | Not established | | Ents | Not established | Not established | | Centaurs | Not established | Not established | | Merfolk | Not established | Not established | | Giants | Not established | Not established | | Living Mountains | Number unknown | Individual dormancy may last centuries or millennia; lifespan unknown | | Human cultures | Not established | Not established | | Sentient animal peoples | Not established | Not established | ## Shared antiquity and historical uncertainty Khazari and Eldar are both ancient peoples. There is no universally accepted creation story establishing which came first. Do not give either people unquestioned primacy in Eryndor's origin history. The deeper origins, first appearances, ancient migrations and full population histories of many peoples remain unresolved. Different cultures may preserve conflicting traditions. Such traditions should be attributed to their sources rather than presented as universally confirmed history. ## Roleplaying and worldbuilding guidance - Give each NPC an individual personality, motive, flaw, loyalty and history. - Species reputation is a starting expectation, not a script. - Regional culture, class, profession, faith, education, family and personal experiences all matter. - Let characters contradict stereotypes naturally. - Do not use species as a shortcut for moral alignment, intelligence or worth. - A people can have multiple societies, political factions, dialects and internal disagreements. - When developing a new people, establish its ecology, society, history and relationships without assuming it must resemble a familiar fantasy template. ## Small communities and scattered settlements Not every people in Eryndor belongs to a great kingdom, city or unified civilisation. The world should also contain small villages, hamlets, hidden steadings, burrow-settlements, woodland enclaves, cave communities and other modest homes belonging to lesser magical peoples and other small-scale communities. These settlements may be scattered across forests, woodlands, plains, hills, marshes, mountain valleys, underground passages and caverns, and suitable coastal, island or underwater environments. Some may be close to major roads or larger settlements; others may be remote, concealed, seasonal or accessible only through local knowledge. Their scale and way of life should suit the people, habitat and available resources. A settlement does not need to be a sovereign nation or have a formal ruler. It may be a family cluster, a few neighbouring households, a clan hamlet, a market village, a network of burrows or a small community connected to nearby settlements by custom, trade, kinship or mutual protection. Some communities may be mixed; others may be predominantly one people. This is established world canon. The nine additional peoples have suitable small communities where habitat, ecology and geography support them. Additional peoples beyond this roster still require explicit approval. The individual settlement patterns, named villages, locations, populations and political relationships of any approved entries remain to be developed where not already specified. Do not invent named settlements or precise map placements and present them as previously established. ## Additional peoples — established canon The following nine peoples are established inhabitants of Eryndor: Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies. The descriptions and cultural concepts in this chapter are current canon and may be revised, expanded, replaced or retconned by the creator at any time. Details explicitly marked unknown or unresolved remain open; canon status does not require inventing answers to unanswered biological, historical or cultural questions. Each people includes individuals of varied character and morality. ### Kobolds — established people Core concept: Small, intelligent, scaled folk adapted to enclosed spaces, rough terrain and communal construction. They should be a real people rather than disposable trap-making nuisances. Provisional biology: Generally short, light-framed and agile, with overlapping scales, strong hands, clawed fingers and keen low-light vision. Their exact appearance may vary between lineages and regions. Their exact thermal physiology remains unresolved; whether they are fully warm-blooded or partially temperature-sensitive has not been decided. In either case, avoid making them implausibly comfortable in every climate. Their size may help in narrow passages but should limit reach, carrying capacity and direct physical contests with larger folk. Their senses, diet, reproduction and lifespan remain open. Societies: Some communities could live in natural caverns, old quarries, cliff warrens, dry ravines or carefully engineered burrow networks. Others might build surface hamlets around workshops, kilns or mines. Cooperative engineering, water management, ventilation, storage and shared maintenance could be central to some cultures, while others are pastoral, trading or itinerant. A kobold community may be meticulous and safety-conscious; another may be a chaotic collection of brilliant improvisers. Character and humour: Practical, inventive, socially observant and sometimes suspicious of outsiders. Their humour can involve elaborate warning signs, petty engineering rivalries and arguments over whose tunnel is technically the main entrance. Do not make all kobolds cowardly, greedy, trap-obsessed or obsessed with dragons. Open design questions: How closely, if at all, do they associate with Drakari? Are there major regional lineages? What are their actual thermal needs and lifespan? ### Satyrs / Fauns — established people Core concept: A people with humanlike upper bodies and caprine lower limbs, adapted to woodland margins, hills, rocky slopes and open pastoral country. Satyr and faun may be regional names, related cultural branches or two distinct peoples; that distinction is not yet decided. Provisional biology: Digitigrade legs, cloven hooves, balance suited to uneven ground, and digestive systems adapted to a mixed diet with substantial plant matter. Horns, ears, coats and body proportions may vary. Their agility should be terrain-dependent rather than supernatural: excellent on broken slopes and woodland paths, less suited to deep water, smooth floors or heavy armour. Avoid assuming every individual is musical, intoxicated or sexually mischievous. Societies: Possible forms include seasonal woodland villages, hill hamlets, orchard communities, shepherding clans, travelling performers, herbalist settlements and permanent market villages. Some may maintain carefully negotiated boundaries with farmers and forest peoples; others may be integrated into larger towns. Music, dance, storytelling, horticulture and animal husbandry can be important in some communities without defining all of them. Character and humour: Sociable traditions may coexist with serious law, land stewardship, family obligations and old grudges. A village may host exuberant seasonal festivals but take water rights, grazing boundaries and hospitality rules extremely seriously. Open design questions: Whether Satyrs and Fauns are one people or related peoples; horn variation; diet and digestive limits; family structure and lifespan. ### Pixies — established people Core concept: Very small, winged, fully intelligent people. Their small size should shape architecture, transport, food requirements and vulnerability without making them childlike or inconsequential. Provisional biology: Lightweight bodies and wings capable of powered flight over limited distances, with flight constrained by weather, fatigue, injury and carried weight. Small body mass creates high heat-loss and energy demands; frequent feeding and sheltered resting places are plausible. Wings should be biological structures with believable attachment and musculature, not effortless magical hover engines. Whether all pixies can fly, and whether wing forms vary, remains open. Societies: Small canopy settlements, hollow-tree chambers, cliff gardens, reed-bed villages, flower-meadow hamlets and concealed structures among larger settlements are possible. Their homes may use lightweight materials, woven fibres, resin, leaf structures and tiny tools. Some communities may trade in specialist knowledge, pollination services, fine craft or messages; others may avoid outsiders. Character and humour: Pixie mischief can be clever social play, protest, practical jokes or a defence against intruders—not random cruelty. A sign moved a few feet, a missing button or a traveller sent along the scenic path can be funny; stealing medicine or leading someone into mortal danger has real consequences. Pixies can also be serious historians, diplomats, gardeners or guardians. Open design questions: Wing anatomy and flight endurance; whether magic is required for flight; how they interact with Aelwyn Fae; lifespan and reproductive biology. ### Minotaurs — established people Core concept: A powerful, horned, bovine-featured people with their own complex societies. They should not be reduced to maze guardians or inherently violent brutes. Provisional biology: Large, muscular humanoid bodies with bovine heads, horns, hooves or broad cloven feet, substantial neck and shoulder musculature, and senses adapted to their environment. Horn shape may vary by lineage, sex, age or individual, but do not assume a single universal pattern. Their size and mass require substantial food, water and space; heat management and joint stress matter. Their anatomy should make clothing, tools, stairs, doorways and transport distinct from human norms. Societies: Some may build broad-street towns, fortified hill settlements, agricultural villages or stone-built communities at crossroads. Others may be mobile pastoralists or members of mixed urban populations. Architecture may favour courtyards, open halls, broad entrances and durable surfaces. Labyrinthine buildings could be cultural, defensive or ceremonial in some regions, but should not define every minotaur settlement. Character and humour: Directness, physical confidence or a reputation for being difficult to move may feature in some cultures, but individuals vary widely. A minotaur architect might be obsessed with elegant wayfinding precisely because outsiders keep assuming every building is a maze. Open design questions: Exact body size range, horn biology, diet, lifespan, birth and family patterns, and whether there are distinct regional peoples under the minotaur name. ### Brownies and Boggarts — established people; relationship unresolved Core concept: Two related small household and landscape peoples in folklore, potentially close relatives or culturally linked branches. Their exact relationship remains undecided. They must be people with agency, not invisible servants or automatic household spirits. Provisional biology: Small-bodied, largely terrestrial folk able to live in human- or dwarf-scale buildings, barns, root-cellars, hedgerows and small burrows. Adaptations may include quiet movement, excellent hearing and comfort in sheltered low-light spaces. Their biology should not require them to vanish, become intangible or work without rest. The names Brownie and Boggart may describe different lineages, local labels or social roles rather than fixed moral categories. Societies: Some Brownie communities may live in small hamlets near farms, mills, stables or villages, maintaining discreet trade and neighbourly agreements. Some Boggart communities may prefer abandoned structures, old boundary places, hedgerows or isolated homesteads. Both may have family networks, local councils, customs and their own economies. Helping with repairs or animal care should be a negotiated relationship, never an assumed obligation. Character and humour: Brownies might be proud of reliable workmanship and deeply offended by being treated as free labour. Boggarts might enjoy unsettling noises, rearranging tools or exposing a household's bad habits. Neither category is morally uniform: a brownie can be a scoundrel, a boggart a loyal neighbour. Open design questions: Whether these are biological relatives, distinct peoples or names imposed by outsiders; how visible they are; what they eat; and whether they possess any innate magic. ### Ogres — established people Core concept: A large-bodied, intelligent people with varied communities, not a synonym for stupid monster. Provisional biology: Robust, heavy-framed humanoids with high caloric and water requirements, strong musculature and physical adaptations suited to carrying loads and traversing rough country. Their size brings trade-offs: greater food needs, difficulty with small structures, heat stress and slower recovery from some injuries. Avoid making them uniformly gigantic; a plausible range of body sizes and regional variation is preferable. Societies: Some may live in extended-family villages, mountain-valley hamlets, forest-edge settlements or river communities. Others may be integrated into larger towns as builders, quarry workers, ferrymen, farmers, guards, cooks or artisans. Their architecture and tools should be scaled to local needs, with mixed-size public spaces where communities interact with smaller peoples. Character and humour: A culture might prize generous hospitality and enormous communal meals, while another values quiet scholarship or careful craftsmanship. Humour can arise from scale mismatches and assumptions, not from making ogres stupid. A master negotiator or meticulous clockmaker is entirely possible. Open design questions: Average height and mass; diet and food production; lifespan; whether ogres are closely related to any other large peoples; and regional variation. ### Trolls — established people Core concept: A diverse people adapted to harsh, damp, rocky, cold or otherwise demanding environments. Their folklore reputation for being dangerous or difficult to kill should not become universal biology. Provisional biology: Heavy, resilient bodies with thick skin, strong connective tissue and adaptations to particular climates. Some lineages may have slow metabolisms or long periods of torpor; others may be active year-round. Regeneration, if included, must have strict biological limits, costs and failure conditions. No automatic limb regrowth or immunity to ordinary weapons. Trolls should not all turn to stone in sunlight; any light sensitivity or environmental vulnerability should be regional and specific. Societies: Bridge-side hamlets, mountain settlements, river-valley villages, cold-region steadings and cave communities are possibilities. Some may maintain toll rights, ferries, stonework, fishing grounds or seasonal grazing routes. Others may live in ordinary mixed settlements. A troll village could be known for bridge engineering, patient dispute resolution or a very strict policy about littering in the river. Character and humour: Some trolls may be taciturn and slow to trust; others sociable, scholarly or theatrical. A reputation for guarding bridges could arise from a few local customs or historical agreements, not a universal instinct. Open design questions: Which lineages, if any, regenerate; metabolism and dormancy; sunlight tolerance; lifespan; and the origins of regional troll folklore. ### Mushroom folk — established people Core concept: A people whose bodies are fungal or fungus-like, with varied forms and a life cycle fundamentally different from animal peoples. They should not be walking mushrooms with a single shared mind or personality. Provisional biology: Bodies may combine a visible fruiting structure with a more substantial living body and rootlike or mycelial tissues. They may exchange nutrients through fungal networks, symbiosis or cultivated substrates. Their needs could include moisture, minerals, organic matter and particular temperature ranges. Reproduction may involve spores, budding or other processes, but spore release should not automatically infect, control or transform other peoples. Individual identity, memory and consent must remain clear unless a specific culture or biology deliberately complicates them. Societies: Communities may grow into living architecture in damp forests, old roots, caves, wetlands and underground chambers. Some could cultivate orchards, decay fallen timber, manage soil fertility or maintain underground gardens. Their settlements might be seasonal or move slowly as their growing substrate changes. Trade could involve medicines, dyes, preserved foods, cultivation knowledge and materials. Character and humour: Some communities may be contemplative and patient; others argumentative, entrepreneurial, gossipy or extremely competitive about cultivation. A mushroom-folk village can have politics, gossip and a terrible local theatre troupe like anyone else. Open design questions: Individual lifespan and continuity; whether mycelial networks share information or consciousness; spore safety; mobility; food and water requirements; and how reproduction works. ### Harpies — established people Core concept: A winged, avian-featured intelligent people adapted to cliffs, highlands, sea stacks and open-air settlements. They are not simply bird monsters or universally predatory. Provisional biology: Humanlike or otherwise clearly sapient bodies with feathered wings, strong flight musculature, light but durable skeletons and specialised respiratory and balance systems. True powered flight imposes strict limits on body mass, wing area, take-off space and carried loads. Large individuals may glide more easily than they can take off from flat ground. Hands, feet and wing anatomy need a deliberate design decision: grasping hands plus wings are possible as fantasy biology, but should be internally consistent and affect tool use. Societies: Cliffside villages, highland hamlets, sea-stack settlements and elevated communal structures are possibilities. Their architecture may use ledges, ramps, windbreaks, rope systems and sheltered landing areas. Some may be coastal fishers, couriers, navigators, shepherds or traders; others may be settled inland communities. Ground-level access and accessibility should be considered in mixed settlements. Character and humour: Singing may be an art, work tradition or regional custom, but not an irresistible biological compulsion. Some harpies may be quiet, some terrible singers, some skilled negotiators or meticulous builders. Their reputation for shrieking or luring travellers could be folklore, propaganda or a description of particular groups—not a universal trait. Open design questions: Wing and hand anatomy; flight limits and body-size range; diet; nesting and family structures; lifespan; and whether regional forms differ substantially. ## Shared canon principles for the nine additional peoples - Kobolds, Satyrs/Fauns, Pixies, Minotaurs, Brownies/Boggarts, Ogres, Trolls, Mushroom folk and Harpies are established peoples of Eryndor. Their current concepts and descriptions are canon, subject to future revision by the creator. - Each people must have believable biology, ecological needs, reproduction and life history, with abilities balanced by meaningful constraints. - Each should contain multiple cultures, settlements, occupations, personalities and political arrangements. No single village or character represents an entire people. - Serious history, ordinary daily life, humour and eccentricity can coexist. Whimsy should not erase danger, agency, dignity or consequences. - Avoid assigning inherent morality, intelligence, temperament or political allegiance by species. - Distinguish innate biological traits from learned skills, cultural customs, magical abilities and outsider stereotypes. - Do not invent precise populations, lifespans, continent-wide ranges, moon affinities, powers or historical origins where they have not yet been established. These details remain open, but the current established traits and reputations should be used consistently unless the user revises them. - Their small villages and hamlets may occur in forests, plains, hills, mountains, underground regions, coasts and oceans where biologically and culturally plausible. No exact named settlements or coordinates are established by these drafts. - Do not silently merge these peoples with Goblins, Gnomes, Halflings, Aelwyn Fae, Merfolk, Giants, Ents or Living Mountains. Any kinship, shared ancestry or political relationship requires its own decision. ## Encounter direction — familiar fantasy danger and rarity of exceptions This section establishes the current canon direction for the nine additional peoples' reputations, behaviour and rarity of unusually kind individuals. These portrayals are part of the setting and may be revised by the creator. No species is inherently good or evil; individual and group behaviour remains grounded in motive, culture, circumstance and choice. Eryndor should retain the familiar emotional language of fantasy folklore and adventure. Readers should recognise the fears, warnings, legends and dangers associated with creatures and peoples. Do not make every familiar fantasy idea morally inverted, harmless, or so nuanced that it loses its dramatic identity. Some creatures really are dangerous; some individuals and groups are malicious; some encounters should be frightening, and retreat may be the sensible response. At the same time, a species' reputation is not an absolute rule about every individual. No species is inherently good or evil. Where trustworthy individuals are described as exceptionally rare, that rarity belongs to a particular local reputation, hostile faction, social norm or historical pattern—not to an innate moral nature shared by the whole people. Communities and individuals may be dangerous, predatory, welcoming, cooperative, cruel or generous, and those patterns can vary by region and circumstance. A rare exception can feel meaningful without turning morality into a biological trait. ### Working reputation and exception spectrum - Ogres: Often dangerous, aggressive or associated with raids on isolated settlements, livestock theft, violence and destruction. Peaceful ogre communities and decent individuals can exist without being extraordinary impossibilities; the degree of danger varies by group and individual. - Harpies: Generally feared as dangerous aerial predators or raiders. Villagers may dread flocks near roads, fields, mountain passes and livestock. A genuinely kind, reliable harpy should be exceptionally rare and likely to challenge strong assumptions. - Minotaurs: Generally intimidating and widely associated in some regions with great physical danger, violent rampages or feared clans and individuals. A peaceful, trustworthy Minotaur should be exceptionally unusual; people may reasonably be frightened or wary before knowing one. - Trolls: Often feared as dangerous, territorial and unpredictable, especially around bridges, caves, rivers and mountain paths. Some may be capable of bargains or peaceful dealings, but danger remains real. - Kobolds: May be regarded as crafty, secretive, troublesome or dangerous around mines, tunnels and warrens. They can also trade, cooperate and form friendships; do not reduce every encounter to a trap or ambush. - Pixies: May be whimsical and mischievous, but their small size should not make them automatically harmless. Pranks, misdirection and luring travellers into danger can feature in folklore and real encounters. - Boggarts: May carry a strong folklore reputation for frightening, unsettling or malicious mischief — the sort of being invoked in warnings to children about strange noises outside at night. Brownies and boggarts need not share the same reputation. - Brownies: May more commonly be associated with helpful household or farmstead folklore, while still having agency, boundaries and the capacity for resentment or wrongdoing. They are not automatic servants. - Satyrs/Fauns: May be known in some places as sociable, charming woodland or pastoral folk, while stories of dangerous invitations, mischief or threatening individuals give travellers reason for caution. - Mushroom folk: May be unfamiliar or unsettling to outsiders, with some communities welcoming and others genuinely strange, secretive or dangerous. Do not make unfamiliarity itself proof of evil. These are broad working reputations and story expectations, not universal facts about every region, settlement or individual. Local folklore may exaggerate, contradict or misunderstand what is actually true. A feared reputation should still have a plausible basis in history, behaviour, dangerous encounters or cultural memory. ### Storytelling principles - Preserve recognisable fantasy folklore: the big bad wolf in the dark woods, warnings about harpies overhead, the Minotaur that tears through a village, and the ogre that raids a farmstead should all feel at home in Eryndor where appropriate. - Do not flatten every people into moral ambiguity. Some individuals, bands, predators or hostile factions can be genuinely malicious and dangerous. - Do not make every member of a feared people evil. A rare exception can be memorable without making the wider reputation meaningless. - Let reputation have practical consequences: frightened villagers, barred gates, warnings to travellers, local customs, patrols, protective measures, rumours and prejudice. - Let the reader and characters encounter both the familiar expectation and the reality behind it. Sometimes the warning is justified; sometimes it is exaggerated; sometimes an unusual individual defies it. - Keep the distinction between intelligent peoples and non-sapient dangerous creatures clear. A frightening encounter need not always involve a person or society. - Do not assume every region has the same experience or opinion. Reputation should develop locally and historically. Guiding balance: Familiar fantasy at its heart, with enough biological, cultural and individual depth to make Eryndor feel like a living world. Nuance should enrich danger and wonder, not erase them.
